content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose the data augmentation method for hypergraphs. 
* The authors divide the original features in the hypergraph into common and personal features, to treat them separately, where one is for node features and the other is for hyperedge features.
* The authors randomly generate masks of common and personal features, to obtain multiple hypergraphs, which are then used to predict the class label of nodes.
* To make the outputs from multiple hypergraphs to be similar, the authors use the consistency regularization loss. 
* The authors evaluate their method on the semi-supervised node classification task, and further show the effectiveness of their methods on over-smoothing and adversarial attack.
content.main_review:
### Strengths
* Data augmentation for hypergraphs is an undiscovered problem, and the authors tackle this.
* Theoretical analysis of over-smoothing on common and personal features is interesting, and the empirical evidence supports the theory.

### Weaknesses
* Novelty is highly limited, since most components in the proposed FAHGNN are highly similar (even exactly the same) to the ones in previous work [1]. Specifically, from the random dropping scheme for node and hyperedge features, to the feature propagation scheme, to the consistency regularization loss are almost similar to the random propagation for graph data augmentation in [1].
* The focus of this work is unclear in the introduction. What is the main focus of this work, among proposing new features for hypergraphs, data augmentation of hypergraphs with random mask, over-smoothing, or robustness against adversarial attacks? The authors start with indicating the over-smoothing problem in deep GNNs, however, they then describe the common and personal features of hypergraphs.
* Theorem 2. and Theorem 3. do not give intuitions for their regularization term, thus two theorems might not necessary to emphasize the strength of it. What is the point that two theorems imply?
* The authors use only one hypergraph dataset, namely 20-newsgroup, while they mainly tackle the hypergraphs, which is not convincing for me. In other words, one dataset is not enough to evaluate the hypergraph method. While the authors modify the existing citation dataset of normal graphs to the hypergraphs, it is more convincing to use more hypergraph-structured datasets.
* The authors claim that the proposed FAHGNN is beneficial to the over-smoothing problem. However, as shown in Figure 2, the performances are dramatically decreasing as the number of layers is increasing. It seems the proposed model does not alleviate the over-smoothing issue.

### Clarity
* How to simultaneously use the personal and common features before applying MLPs? Is this a simple concatenation of them? In equation (3), the authors only describe the common feature matrix, whereas the personal feature matrix is not used to generate outputs.

### Typo
* In the conclusion section, HFAHGNN -> FAHGNN.

---

[1] Feng et al., Graph Random Neural Network for Semi-Supervised Learning on Graphs, NeurIPS 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: The only novel part is the proposal of common and personal features for hypergraphs, however, the other parts are extremely similar to the previous work [1] in the above. Thus, as the novelty is highly limited, I recommend the rejection of this paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the provided comments. 

We want to clarify several wrong understandings about this paper which were written in the Summary Of The Paper.


+ The authors randomly generate masks of common and personal features, to obtain multiple hypergraphs, which are then used to predict the class label of nodes.


+ To make the outputs from multiple hypergraphs to be similar, the authors use the consistency regularization loss.


About the second point, it is right that we randomly generate masks of common and personal features, but it is not to obtain multiple hypergraphs. The hypergraph structure is not changed in our work. 


About the third point, the aim of consistency regularization loss used in the paper is not to make the outputs from multiple hypergraphs to be similar. As we said before, we just have one hypergraph structure. We augment features in this work from two aspects: augmenting the original features into common features and private features; further augmenting features by drop strategy. Leveraging the idea that a classifier should output the same class distribution for an unlabeled example even after it has been augmented, we utilize consistency regularization to enhance similar predictions on multiple augmentations with the two feature types.

content.title: Short clarification
content.comment:
Thank you for your response.
Since the deadline of interaction is fastly approaching, here I would like to quickly clarify my summary, which is correct.

---

1. The hypergraph structure is not changed in our work.

Yes, I already understood that the hypergraph structure is not changed. My intention was that the authors propose to obtain **multiple hypergraph features (i.e., multiple hypergraph augmentations) from the same hypergraph with random masks**.

Let me clarify the term for hypergraphs that I used and you referred.
* For me, if the features of the hypergraphs are different, then they are regarded as the different hypergraphs.
* For authors, if the features of the hypergraph are different while the incidences (structures) of them are the same, then they are regarded as the same hypergraph.

---

2. The aim of the consistency regularization loss used in the paper is not to make the outputs from multiple hypergraphs to be similar.

According to the above response (1.), there are multiple hypergraph features from the same hypergraph, and my summary -- that the authors use the consistency regularization loss to enhance similar predictions across multiple feature outputs (i.e., to make outputs from multiple hypergraph features to be similar) -- is also correct.

---

Note that, since the novelty concern (similar to the existing work GRAND [1]) raised by several reviewers still remains and the authors have not rebutted this, I maintain my score: reject.

---

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks for your response.

**Q1.** The novelty of the proposed method.

We want to clarify the novelty of the proposed FAHGNN, and will give a clear illustration in the next vision.

1. We want to give an analysis of the problem which we focus on in this paper. We expect to improve the expressive power of GNNs, however, it has been pointed out that most GNNs cannot get more powerful representation by stacking more layers as CNNs. Recent researches reported that node representations become indistinguishable (known as over-smoothing) as the network depth increases, in other words, the expressive power of existing deep GNNs is weak. Thus, how to get more powerful expressiveness. For GNNs, the most important two parts are features and graph structures. Targeting on the graph structure, for representation learning, hypergraphs usually have more expressive power than graphs through their ability to encode higher-order data correlations. Therefore, our proposed method is based on the hypergraph structure. Basically, the proposed FAHGNN based on hypergraph is different from GRAND based on the graph.


2. To get more powerful GNNs, we need to address the problem of over-smoothing. 
As for GNNs, graph structure (connections) and the features of the data are two critical components, we can do some works from these two perspectives to address over-smoothing. Focusing on the graph structure, it has shown that the drop strategy [1] is useful, which is the main idea in Dropedge [2] and GRAND [3]. Essentially, let the graph be sparse. However, we should notice that the basis is feature representation, the previous works [4][5] explained over-smoothing from the perspective of feature representation, i.e., the features of nodes become indistinguishable as the depth grows. As feature representation is fundamental, we expect to solve the over-smoothing issue from the perspective of the distinguishable power of feature, which is not be explored.


In the paper, we creatively introduce the common feature and personal feature to show that the different distinguishable power of features. As we defined in the paper, for a node, the common features contain the shared information with other nodes (for hypergraph, it is encoded by hyperedges), while the personal features represent its special information. Common features let nodes indistinguishable and personal features let them distinguishable, thus, it is extremely important to enhance the expressive power of GNNs by introducing these two feature types to replace original features as input features.

 
Then, it is clear that the existing methods expect to get more powerful expressiveness by stacking layers as same as deep CNNs, however, suffering from over-smoothing. As we illustrated before, the different properties of common features and personal features show that these two kinds of features are not both fit for deep propagation. Thus, we design different propagation layers for these two feature types. In the theoretical analysis and experiments, we can find that compared to personal features, with common features as input, GNNs is easier to suffer from over-smoothing.


Based on the hypergraph, the common features are generally encoded by hyperedges. Targeting two kinds of features, we design different propagation rules. Especially, we first proposed the convolutional operation on hyperedge features.


3. As we agreed before, making graphs sparse also helps to alleviate over-smoothing. Therefore, we also integrate some techniques that have been demonstrated useful in other papers, like the drop strategy used in DropEdge and GRAND. Specifically, we augment features by DropFeature to make connections sparse in the propagation procedure. Note that though Dropedge, DropNode, DropFeature have similar motivations, they also have subtle differences. Our proposed DropFeature focuses on features, no matter of edge or node. As for the propagation rules, it should note that the coral point of our proposed methods is the numbers of propagation layers for common features and private features are different, which is important for alleviating over-smoothing. This is different from other existing methods. As consistency regularization is a general ML technique, we utilize it to enhance similar predictions on multiple augmentations with the two feature types. Note that based on the hypergraph, some rules need to be explored again compared to GRAND which is based on a graph. 


Totally, the proposed methods mainly focus on enhancing the expressive power of GNNs and alleviating over-smoothing from the perspective of distinguishable power of features, which has not been explored before. The proposed method can integrate other strategies which are also helpful to mitigate the issues of over-smoothing and non-robustness to show more powerful performance.

I would like to thank the authors for clarifying the novelty of the proposed FAHGNN.

**Regarding Q1.,**

I agree that the proposed work targets the "features" of the "hypergraph", while existing works target the "nodes or edges" of the "graph", thus they have different focuses. content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
**Q2.** The focus of this work.


We mainly focus on improving the expressive power of GNNs. 


1.	Based on the superiority of the hypergraph in encoding high-order correlations, we proposed a framework on hypergraph to obtain a more powerful representation.


2.	As we analyzed in the response of Q1, there are two aspects we can pay attention to addressing over-smoothing to improve the expressive power of the model. In this paper, we expect to solve this issue from the distinguishable power of feature. Thus, we introduce common features and personal features and further augment these two kinds of features in the propagation process, and show the great importance of them in solving over-smoothing from theoretically and experimentally. Therefore, it is clear that we need to explore and exploit the common and personal features of hypergraphs to address the over-smoothing problem in deep GNNs. 


3.	To show the superiority of the proposed method, we evaluate it from multiple aspects including node classification performance, mitigating over-smoothing, more robustness when suffering from attacks.


**Q3.** About Theorem 2. and Theorem 3. 


Theorem 2. and Theorem 3. give the regularization effect of feature augmentation with respect to the consistency loss and supervised loss. Due to the limited space, we didn’t give more illustrations. We will revise them in the next revision.


**Q4.** The hypergraph-structured datasets.


It is difficult to find some hypergraph structure networks with features, though high-order correlations are common in the real world. Even for the networks with an original graph or hypergraph structures, the edges or hyperedges are generated based on relationships or assumptions among objects. For example, the citation datasets create an edge for two papers that have a citation relationship. Thus, based on the citation relationship among multiple papers, it is reasonable to generate hyperedges.


**Q5.** The problem of Figure 2.


Please note that Figure 2 is not the result of our proposed FAHGNN.


Figure 2 shows the classification accuracy of HGNN with different input features on the 20-newsgroup dataset. The accuracy is observed to decrease when the depth of HGNN increases from 2. We can see that these three features achieve comparable results when the number of layers is small. However, with personal features as input features, HGNN can achieve the best training and testing accuracy when the depth is larger than 4. With common features, HGNN achieves the lowest accuracy with 6-layer networks. Thus, it is clear that existing GNNs based on the hypergraph also suffer from serious over-smoothing. Personal features can reduce the convergence speed of over-smoothing compared to common features. Common features usually show better performance in shallow layers, while personal features get advantages in deep layers, therefore, augmenting original features into common and personal features can help mitigate the over-smoothing problem.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2194 by Reviewer pySa

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a feature-augmented hypergraph neural networks (FAHGNN) architecture that takes into account the information of hypergraph structure and data augmentations. It’s demonstrated that the results of FAHGNN are competitive to state-of-the-art baselines. The proposed approach is evaluated on node classification task.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

* Paper is clearly written, the provided figures help understanding.
* The method is simple and elegant. It should be easy to reproduce it. Reasonable baselines are used for comparison. The proposed FAHGNN outperforms state-of-the-art GCN-based models across all four datasets. 
* The proposed method is more robust to random attacks.

---
Weakness:
* The paper has very limited methodological novelty. The authors claim that they first adopt DropFeature by randomly dropping out entire feature vectors of some nodes and hyperedges (in Section 3.2); however, the actual operation of DropFeature takes very similar form from the Feng et al. NeurIPS’21 (GRAND) (where GRAND proposes DropNode via remove some nodes’ entire feature vectors), so I would not evaluate the DropFeature as being a novel contribution. To show the contribution of DropFeature over DropNode, it would be more convincing if the authors can add some experiments to show that DropFeature is substantially an improved version of DropNode; for instance, lower computational complexity, less memory cost, more flexible in dropping features rather than dropping nodes, the difference between the drop rates of DropFeature and DropNode in experiments, etc.

* Since a good (learned) hypergraph structure can represent the data correlation and formulate the relationship among 3D objects well. Given the significance of this paper relies on its empirical evaluation, the experiments of applying hypergraph learning to 3D shape recognition and gesture recognition would be very interesting and need to be explored. Compared with Feng et al. AAAI’19, several experiments (e.g., ModelNet40 and NTU) are missing which should be included in the paper for better understanding of the empirical study of FAHGNN.

* The authors mention they use both supervised loss and consistency regularized loss for better prediction, where the consistency regularization was utilized in Feng et al. NeurIPS’21 (GRAND) and had been proved to be effective for the node classification. However, in the ablation study, this paper does not provide the evidence whether the performances of FAHGNN are rely on the consistency regularization. For instance, the consistency regularization strongly affects the performance of GRAND on citation networks.
 
* The proposed method can only be claimed to outperform existing methods on Cora and 20-newsgroup. To evaluate the efficiency of proposed architecture for the problem of oversmoothing, I’d recommend the authors conduct the same analysis on other citation networks for consistency. For instance, it is interesting to see the results about the effects of two feature types (i.e., common and personal features) and DropFeature technique on the dataset with a large number of features (i.e., Citeseer) which suffer from either oversmoothing or attacks.
 
* It’s unclear how the authors select the optimal hyperparameters of FAHGNN. Also, it’s unclear how to choose common and personal features (with corresponding computational complexity / running time). Also, can the authors add more details about common and personal features selection for each dataset? This is not clear to me.
 
* I also have concerns about whether the FAHGNN can achieve promising results on large networks, e.g., Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) and other benchmarks. Since this paper utilizes the consistency regularization on multiple augmentations among different types of features, it would be interesting to see whether the multiple hyperedge features can help withstand unforeseen corruptions.
 
* I encourage the authors to conduct other adversarial attack strategies (e.g., Metattack (Zügner et al.), Nettack (Zügner et al.), etc.) to show the robustness of the proposed model.
 
* Although the proposed model performs well on all datasets, a more convincing argument could be made here if classification accuracy under different label rates on citation networks was considered.

I will adjust the evaluation score if the authors can show additional experiment results, analyses, and more details on the novelty of this work during the rebuttal period.

---
Other comments:
* For Oversmoothing and robustness analysis (Appendix A.3), there is a typo where the authors claim that the oversmoothing and robustness analysis were conducted on Pubmed, however, the results on 20-newsgroup were shown in Figure 5.

* The notation $C$ is used for (1) the number of classes (in Complexity, Section 3.3), (2) the feature dimension of common feature matrix (in Definition 2, Section 3.4), and (3) dimension of matrices A and B (in Lemma1, Section 3.4).
 
* For the 20-newsgroup dataset, the authors do not provide the size of the training set information.
 
* In Common features and personal features in Appendix A.2, the authors use $\bf{H}_j$ for both common and personal features. The notation $\bf{H}$ is not very clear here.

References

Feng et al. “Hypergraph Neural Networks.” AAAI (2019)

Feng et al. “Graph Random Neural Network for Semi-Supervised Learning on Graphs.” NeurIPS (2021)

Zügner and Günnemann. “Adversarial attacks on graph neural networks via meta learning.” ICLR (2019)

Zügner, Akbarnejad, and Günnemann. “Adversarial attacks on neural networks for graph data.” KDD (2018)
content.summary_of_the_review: The major concern of the paper is the novelty. While the authors propose a method that harnesses several frameworks (e.g., common/personal features, data augmentation with dropping features, and consistency regularization) in the design that are helpful to its success, most of these elements are not new to the literature. Thus, providing insights and demonstrating why the design should work is more important. However, I find there is a lack of justification and insights in explaining why the proposed method should work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the provided comments. Those comments are valuable and very helpful for improving our paper. We hopefully clarify the motivation to address the misunderstanding in Q1.


**Q1.**  About "first".


1. DropFeature is not our main contribution. For graph neural networks, there are two important components, one is the graph structure (connections), the other is the features of the data. To alleviate the over-smoothing, we can do some works from these two perspectives. Focusing on the graph structure, it has shown that the drop strategy [1] is useful, which is the main idea in Dropedge [2] and GRAND [3]. Essentially, let the graph be sparse. However, we should notice that the basis is feature representation, the previous works [4] [5] explained over-smoothing from the perspective of feature representation, i.e., the features of nodes become indistinguishable as the depth grows. As feature representation is fundamental, we expect to alleviate the over-smoothing issue from the perspective of the distinguishable power of feature, which is not be explored.


2. Further, to address over-smoothing, considering graph connections and feature representation are both significant. Thus, the FAHGNN also integrates some techniques such as drop strategy to consider graph connections.


3. We hopefully address the misunderstanding of “first”. The “first” here is not claimed the drop strategy is first proposed in this work. The “first” means we adopt DropFeature as the first step in Information Propagation. It is clear that DropFeature is motivated by drop strategy [1], similar to dropedge used in Dropedge [2] and DropNode used in GRAND [3].


4. We would like to further explain the differences of DropFeature in this work with DropNode in GRAND. While DropFeature, DropNode, Dropedge are all motivated by drop strategy, there are subtle differences among them. As I said before, DropEdge and GRAND expect to sparse the graph with drop edges and drop node features, respectively. What we focus on is the feature, no matter of node or edge, DropFeature drops the features of node and edges to augment features in order to get a more powerful representation.

As we said before, making the graph structure sparse can help to alleviate over-smoothing. Thus, the large network doesn’t mean it is easy to suffer from over-smoothing, in contrast, the small datasets with more connections are often limited in over-smoothing with stacking more layers. We will try to give the results, but please note this experimental result does not affect the conclusion of this paper.


**Q7.** More Experiments about attacking.

Though it is interesting to see more results, this paper is not mainly focusing on attacking. We will try to give some results.


**Q8.** More Experiments about different label rates.


Different label rates may have an influence on the performance if we use less labeled data. But in fact, the superiority of our proposed methods is obvious because we introduce more information by augmentation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a novel regularization method for training hypergraph neural networks.
content.main_review:
The proposed approach augments feature representations by introducing common features for modeling shared information between nodes in a hyperedge, and personal features for capturing differences between the nodes. The proposed method also randomly drops node features during the propagation process. Yet another method used in the proposed method is to mix k-order propagation features to obtain augmented node features. All these methods can help to combat over-smoothing of (hyper)GNN learning. 

The results show that the proposed FAHGNN (feature augmented hypergraph neural network) achieves best performance in comparison to other competing methods. Overall, it is a nice paper. I thought the clarity on the experimental results can be improved. For example, on 20-newsgroup dataset, dropout alone seems to provides pretty good results already. Similarly, the GRAND method that relies on a random regularizer achieves pretty close results. The additional benefits brought by personal features do not seem that significant anymore. Better explanations or more clear results would be helpful.

content.title: Response to Reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks for your positive evaluation and insightful feedback. Below we address specific questions.

**Q1.** The similar performance of FAHGNN_drop  with FAHGNN.


We are sorry about the unclear illustration of FAHGNN_drop. Please note that the only difference between FAHGNN with FAHGNN_drop is that in the information propagation process, FAHGNN adopts dropping some nodes’ entire vectors while FAHGNN_drop directly adopts dropout strategy [1] for the feature matrix. Thus, these two methods can achieve similar performance. Similar results show that the choice of drop strategies is not the critical factor for the performance of the proposed FAHGNN on 20-newsgroup. 


[1] Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting. JMLR, 2014. 


**Q2.** The good performance of GRAND.


We would give more explanations about why GRAND also achieves pretty close results with the proposed FAHGNN_personal on Cora or Citeseer.


From the perspective of graph structure, GRAND is based on the graph Laplacian convolution while FAHGNN_personal is based on the hypergraph Laplacian convolution. GCN and HGNN are two methods based on graph Laplacian and hypergraph Laplacian, respectively. It is clear that HGNN achieve a 0.1% improvement compared to GCN on Cora. Therefore, the hypergraph doesn’t show its superiority and we cannot ignore the difficulty of further improving the performance on certain datasets such as Cora. 


On the other hand, the ways of choosing personal features also have an influence on the performance of FAHGNN_personal. We will explore more methods to obtain personal information from original features.
